title: Getting Started with Next.js 15 App Router
excerpt: A practical walkthrough of server components, layouts, and the new caching model.
content:
The App Router changes the default mental model: every component is a Server Component unless you opt into "use client". That means data fetching can happen directly inside the component with async/await, no useEffect or loading state required for the initial render.

Layouts (`layout.tsx`) wrap nested routes and persist across navigations, so shared chrome like a navbar doesn't re-render on every page change. Route segments can also export `loading.tsx` and `error.tsx`, which React Suspense and error boundaries pick up automatically.

One breaking change worth calling out: in recent versions `params` and `searchParams` passed to Server Components are Promises and must be awaited before use. Skipping this either throws or silently returns a Promise object instead of the value you expect, so it's the first thing to check when a dynamic route behaves oddly.

For this project, `app/posts/[id]/page.tsx` fetches the post directly via the Firestore Admin SDK on the server, and passes the result to a client component as SWR's `fallbackData` so the browser doesn't need to refetch on mount.

title: Why We Chose SWR + Zustand Over Redux
excerpt: A breakdown of server state vs. client state, and why we split the two.
content:
Server state and client state solve different problems, and conflating them under one store is where a lot of Redux boilerplate comes from. SWR handles fetching, caching, and revalidating data that lives on the server — posts, comments — while Zustand holds transient UI state that never touches the network: filters, modals, form drafts.

This split keeps each tool doing one job well, and cuts most of the action/reducer/selector boilerplate that a single global store tends to accumulate over time. SWR gives us request deduplication, stale-while-revalidate caching, and automatic revalidation after mutations basically for free. Zustand gives us a tiny, hook-based store for UI state without the ceremony of actions and reducers.

The trade-off is discipline: it's tempting to shove server data into Zustand "just this once." We enforce the boundary by convention — anything that could be fetched from `/api/*` lives in a `hooks/useX.ts` SWR hook, and anything that's purely local UI state lives in `store/`.

title: Modeling Comments as a Firestore Subcollection
excerpt: Trade-offs of subcollections vs. top-level collections for nested data.
content:
Firestore gives you two reasonable ways to model comments on a post: a top-level `comments` collection with a `postId` field, or a `posts/{postId}/comments` subcollection. We went with the subcollection.

The main win is locality: fetching a post's comments is a scoped query with no `where` clause needed, and deleting a post's comments when the post is deleted is a matter of deleting everything under that path rather than running a filtered query across a much larger collection. Security rules are also simpler to reason about, since `resource.data` inside a subcollection rule already has an implicit relationship to its parent document.

The trade-off is that queries spanning comments *across* posts (e.g., "all comments by user X") require a collection group query instead of a normal collection query. For this project's scope — a single-post comment thread — that trade-off is the right one.

We also maintain a denormalized `commentCount` field on the post document, incremented and decremented inside the same Route Handler that writes the comment, so the post list can show a comment count without a separate read per post.

title: Securing Route Handlers with Firebase Auth
excerpt: Verifying ID tokens on the server and enforcing ownership rules.
content:
Every mutating Route Handler in this app follows the same shape: read the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header, verify it with `adminAuth.verifyIdToken(token)`, and reject with 401 if it's missing or invalid. That gives us a trusted `uid` for the rest of the handler.

Ownership checks come next and are separate from authentication: being logged in proves who you are, it doesn't prove you're allowed to edit a specific post. `PATCH` and `DELETE` handlers load the target document first and compare `doc.authorId === uid` before making any write. The same rule is duplicated in Firestore Security Rules as a second line of defense, in case a write ever reaches Firestore directly instead of through a Route Handler.

On the client, `lib/api/client.ts` centralizes attaching the current user's ID token to every mutating request, so components never touch tokens directly — they just call `updatePost(id, data)` and the token comes along for free.

title: A Responsive Grid Without Tailwind
excerpt: Building adaptive layouts with plain CSS Modules and container queries.
content:
Dropping Tailwind in favor of CSS Modules doesn't mean giving up a systematic approach to responsive design — it means writing the system by hand instead of importing it.

We define breakpoint values once as CSS custom properties in `globals.css` (`--bp-sm`, `--bp-md`, `--bp-lg`) and reference them consistently across modules. The post grid itself uses `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(280px, 1fr))`, which adapts the column count to available width without a single media query — it naturally collapses to one column on a 375px viewport and three on a 1440px one.

Where a true breakpoint is needed (e.g., collapsing the filter bar into a stacked layout on mobile), we use standard `@media (max-width: 640px)` blocks scoped to that component's module. Nothing here is exotic; it's the same responsive toolkit Tailwind wraps, applied directly.
